questions.q: What is the core purpose of a timelock delay in governance?
options: To speed up how quickly proposals can execute
To prevent any proposal from ever being voted on
To replace the need for voting entirely
To give token holders a window to react after a proposal passes but before it actually takes effect
questions.explain: A timelock is the last line of defense: it gives holders time to notice and react to a queued change -- malicious, buggy, or just a bad idea -- before it executes.

questions.q: Per Aave's Execution Network diagram shown in this lesson, why does the system use two different executor delay tiers instead of one?
options: Two tiers are required by Ethereum itself
The riskier the blast radius of a change (e.g. protocol changes vs. governance config), the longer the delay token holders get to react
One tier is for testnet and the other for mainnet only
There is no reason -- both tiers always use the same delay
questions.explain: Executor lvl1 uses a shorter delay for lower-risk governance config changes; Executor lvl2 uses a longer delay for changes to the protocol itself.

questions.q: In the real Tally screenshot shown in this lesson, what does a proposal tagged QUEUED and ON-CHAIN represent?
options: A proposal that has not yet started voting
A proposal that was permanently rejected
A proposal that passed its vote and is sitting inside its timelock delay, before Execute can be pressed
A proposal that executed instantly with no delay
questions.explain: QUEUED/ON-CHAIN is the state between voting ending and the timelock delay elapsing -- Execute becomes callable only once that delay has passed.

questions.q: In a 3-of-5 multisig treasury, what happens if one signer's private key is compromised?
options: The attacker still needs 2 more legitimate signatures -- the transaction cannot execute from the compromised key alone
The attacker can immediately drain the treasury
The multisig becomes permanently frozen
All 5 signers lose access simultaneously
questions.explain: A 3-of-5 multisig requires any 3 of 5 signatures -- a single compromised key cannot execute a transaction on its own.

questions.q: What do TimelockController's PROPOSER_ROLE, EXECUTOR_ROLE, and CANCELLER_ROLE accomplish, per this lesson's illustration?
options: They are all granted to the exact same address by design
They only exist to track gas usage
They replace the need for a DAO vote entirely
They separate who can queue an action, who can execute it, and who can cancel it, instead of trusting one address with everything
questions.explain: Role separation means proposing, executing, and cancelling are distinct permissions -- commonly: Governor proposes, anyone can execute after the delay, and a security council can cancel.
